gloss: Discussing terms until both sides can agree.
examples: *Bargaining* over the price took an hour.
The union is back at the *bargaining* table.
Hard *bargaining* got them a better deal.

gloss: Arguing back and forth over a price.
examples: After ten minutes of *haggling* he took forty dollars.
There's no *haggling* at a chain store.
*Haggling* is expected at the flea market.

gloss: A point in talks where neither side will move.
examples: The talks reached a *deadlock* over wages.
A mediator finally broke the *deadlock*.
Two *deadlocks* delayed the contract for months.

gloss: The gripping of hands that seals a greeting or an agreement.
examples: The whole deal started with a *handshake*.
They closed it on a *handshake*, with nothing in writing.
A few *handshakes* and the meeting was over.

gloss: Money a company pays to support an event in return for advertising.
examples: The team lost its biggest *sponsorship*.
She signed two *sponsorships* after the win.
*Sponsorships* from local businesses pay for the festival.

gloss: A customer's public statement praising a product or service.
examples: The website is full of customer *testimonials*.
They filmed a *testimonial* with a longtime client.
One good *testimonial* sells more than an ad.

gloss: A small part of the market that one product serves especially well.
examples: They found a *niche* selling gear for left-handed golfers.
The magazine serves a narrow *niche*.
Small *niches* can be very profitable.
contrast: Americans usually say NICH, rhyming with *itch*; the British say NEESH.

gloss: Keeping customers or workers from leaving.
examples: Employee *retention* is their biggest problem.
The discount is aimed at customer *retention*.
*Retention* improved once they raised pay.

gloss: The sending of a customer to a business, or the customer sent that way.
examples: Most of her work comes from *referrals*.
We give a discount for every *referral*.
The *referral* came from a neighbor.

gloss: A possible customer, or a chance that something good will happen.
examples: The salesman had forty *prospects* on his list.
She's a serious *prospect*, not just a browser.
The *prospects* for a deal look better this week.

gloss: The quality of being believed and trusted by others.
examples: The recall cost the company its *credibility*.
She has real *credibility* with customers.
Missing two deadlines hurt his *credibility*.

gloss: The good name a business has built up, counted as part of its value.
examples: Most of the purchase price was *goodwill*.
Years of fair dealing built up a lot of *goodwill*.
They refunded him as a gesture of *goodwill*.

gloss: The gradual introduction of a new product or system.
examples: The *rollout* starts in three cities.
The software *rollout* was a mess.
They planned two *rollouts* for the fall.

gloss: Following the rules and laws that apply to a business.
examples: *Compliance* costs them two full-time employees.
The bank was fined for poor *compliance*.
She works in *compliance* at an insurance company.

gloss: Official proof that a person or product meets a standard.
examples: The plant lost its safety *certification*.
He's working on two *certifications* this year.
The *certification* takes about six weeks.

gloss: A company's order for customers to return an unsafe product.
examples: The *recall* covers two million cars.
There have been three *recalls* this year.
Check whether your model is part of the *recall*.
contrast: The noun is stressed in front (REE-kawl); the verb is rih-KAWL.

gloss: The taking on of new employees.
examples: *Hiring* slowed down after the merger.
The company put a freeze on *hiring*.
*Hiring* is up across the industry.

gloss: The work of finding and hiring new people.
examples: *Recruitment* is handled by an outside firm.
They spent a fortune on *recruitment* last year.
Nurse *recruitment* has gotten much harder.

gloss: Someone whose job is finding people to fill open positions.
examples: A *recruiter* messaged me on Monday.
*Recruiters* get paid when you take the job.
She's a technical *recruiter* for a software company.

gloss: A recruiter who finds senior people, often by tempting them away from other companies.
examples: A *headhunter* called him about a job in Denver.
*Headhunters* charge a big fee.
They hired a *headhunter* to find a new director.

gloss: Providing a business with the workers it needs.
examples: *Staffing* is tight on weekends.
The hospital uses a *staffing* agency.
Poor *staffing* is why the lines are so long.

gloss: Someone who formally asks for a job, a loan, or a place.
examples: We got two hundred *applicants* for one opening.
Every *applicant* takes a short test.
The strongest *applicant* turned us down.

gloss: A short period of work done to gain experience, often for little or no pay.
examples: She did an *internship* at a marketing firm.
The *internship* runs from June to August.
Paid *internships* are hard to find.

gloss: An extra benefit that comes with a job.
examples: Free parking is the best *perk* here.
The pay is average, but the *perks* are good.
One *perk* of the job is the travel.

gloss: Money paid to an employee who is let go.
examples: He got six months of *severance*.
The company offered *severance* to anyone who left early.
*Severance* isn't required by law in most states.

gloss: The removing of someone from a job.
examples: The *dismissal* came without warning.
She's fighting her *dismissal* in court.
Three *dismissals* followed the investigation.
